The sky appears blue because of a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering. Sunlight, which contains all colors of the visible spectrum, enters Earth's atmosphere and collides with tiny gas molecules like nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules scatter shorter wavelengths of light—blue and violet—far more effectively than longer wavelengths like red and orange. Because blue light is scattered roughly ten times more than red, it gets spread in every direction across the sky, making the whole sky glow blue when you look away from the sun. We don't typically perceive the sky as violet, which scatters even more, because our eyes are less sensitive to violet light and a portion of it is absorbed by the upper atmosphere. At sunset, the light travels through a much thicker layer of air, scattering away most of the blue and leaving the warmer reds and oranges we see on the horizon.
